The emails claimed responsibility for a wave of false threats that, between Nov. 3 and Nov. 6, targeted at least 35 passenger flights across Europe. On Nov. 5 alone, around 20 civilian aircraft were affected: Italian, French, and Bulgarian fighter jets scrambled to escort airliners, and an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a French military air base. Italian schools had already been targeted on Oct. 19 and again on Nov. 2, when an email with the same text reached nearly 280 education facilities. In October, hundreds of schools in Britain, Hungary, and Serbia received similar threats.

Some European intelligence officials consider Russia the most likely origin based on motive, modus operandi, and precedent. At the same time, these officials warn that a firm attribution may never come. Naturally, Moscow has denied involvement.

Until a few weeks ago, the debate on Russia’s attacks on Europe was about the violent end of the spectrum: explosive-laden drones targeting a cargo plane in Leipzig, Germany; sabotage of railroad systems in Germany, the Netherlands, and Poland; drones over airports and military bases. These operations crossed into direct physical attacks and required capabilities that few actors possess. The past month shows the opposite end. A hoax bomb threat requires an email account and a few minutes, whereas the cost for the target is enormous: evacuations, bomb-disposal teams, aircraft diversions, fighter-jet scrambles, lost school days, and frightened parents. The authors of the “Message to the West” boasted of having caused widespread panic and forcing European authorities to spend a fortune on their emergency procedures.

This perfectly illustrates the asymmetry of hybrid threats. The defender cannot dismiss the threat because of its potential catastrophic impact, so every hoax triggers the full precautionary protocol. The attacker sets the tempo while the defender can only react and bear the cost.

A second feature makes this part of the hybrid war harder to counter. Schools, airports, and shopping centers in Europe receive their constant dose of empty threats from pranksters, students hoping to skip an exam, extortionists, and people with personal grievances. Each false alarm shows others how easy it is to cause disruption for free. On Wednesday, Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto predicted that such hoaxers will only multiply. Some of the threats against passenger flights claimed to come from the Male State, an anti-feminist movement banned in Russia. The claim of origin reads as mockery but also makes a point: No matter who is behind them, the hoaxes absorb resources and reinforce the perception of insecurity. For an attacker, each new campaign builds on the destabilizing effects of all previous ones.

This is why the low end of the attack spectrum is a useful reminder of what hybrid campaigns are for. Their purpose is psychological, the target is public opinion, and the objective is to generate confusion, fear, and distrust in institutions. A drone strike and a fake email serve the same purpose by different means. The first tests how far the threshold of attacks that Europe will tolerate without responding has moved. The second shows how little it takes to make citizens feel unprotected. Meloni put it plainly on Wednesday: The threats, she said, appear to be part of a strategy to generate alarm and concern.

The hoaxes also expose the attribution problem more starkly than sabotage does. Attribution is both a technical and a political issue. Pure data and forensic analysis rarely provide certainty about the sender. The senders of this month’s threatening emails have worn three masks: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards on Nov. 2, the Male State on Nov. 5, and a pseudonym evoking a long-dead Soviet leader since Nov. 6. Some of last week’s emails to airports came from an address at a public health network in the Colombian capital, Bogotá.

And even when the attack’s origin is clear, government leaders often lack the political will to name the attacker. The reason usually given is fear of escalation. A second reason is rarely admitted: Naming the attacker would mean telling their publics that Russia has already escalated a war against Europe, and that this war demands a response.

This creates a hard problem for policy. Against a threat with such disproportionate costs for the attacker and defender, reactive defense is a losing strategy. This is especially true given the fact that widely accessible technology makes these attacks ever cheaper to carry out at scale. The logical answer is deterrence, which means raising the cost and risk for the attacker. But deterrence rests on attribution, which will often be only partial.

A credible deterrent posture therefore requires a degree of political courage that European governments have so far avoided. It means saying, in advance and together: We may not know with certainty who is behind the next wave, but if it happens, we will impose costs based on the available evidence, even if that evidence is incomplete. This is a probabilistic standard of response, closer to how intelligence works than how courts work. It is uncomfortable for democracies bound by the rule of law and accustomed to standards of incontrovertible evidence. And it carries a risk of error. The alternative is the certain continuation of a campaign that costs an adversary nothing and undermines the target every time.

The posture must also be Europe-wide rather than national. A campaign that reaches Italian schools, Irish newsrooms, and Czech airports in the same week is designed to exploit divisions. A response that each country calibrates on its own invites the attacker to probe for the weakest link.

The final element is speed. Because hybrid campaigns rely on diffused costs and dispersed information, they have to be met with rapid information sharing. When thousands of schools receive the same threatening email at the same moment—and that fact is known within minutes by everyone concerned—then the threat largely diagnoses itself: It is a coordinated campaign, and the alarms are very likely false. Italy’s education minister, Giuseppe Valditara, said as much on Wednesday, noting that the sheer number of schools involved demonstrated how little credibility the threat had.

A similar logic applies to real attacks. When hackers took control of refrigeration systems in hundreds of French supermarkets in October and in stores across at least 11 European countries in early November, the pattern was the clue: It was a simultaneous, automated, and cross-border effort. A shared picture in real time turns hundreds of isolated emergencies into a single recognizable event. It speeds up the response, lowers the payoff for the attacker, and eases the attribution on which deterrence depends. At the European level, most of this civilian information sharing and coordination infrastructure does not yet exist.

In the last two months, we have witnessed two very different ways in which hybrid campaigns exploit free societies as targets for attack. At one end, Europe’s adversaries are testing how much violence it will absorb before it reacts. At the other, they show how cheaply European societies can be disrupted. Both types of attacks are aimed at citizens’ confidence that their institutions can protect them. Europe can answer at both ends, but only if it finds the unity and political will to do it.

Beniamino Irdi is a nonresident senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, the founder and CEO of HighGround, and a former Italian government official.

#5955. Jeffries shredded over Hegseth impeachment snafu as Dem jockeys for speaker’s gavel

Back-to-back blunders on the House floor are raising questions over whether Democrats are ready for primetime as they're poised to take over the majority — and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., makes a bid for the top role.

Democrats are projected to win 255 House seats, with 12 races yet to be called, and Jeffries is running to be Speaker of the House following the sweeping victories last week that saw the party make gains even in traditional Republican strongholds like Texas, Mississippi, Kansas and South Carolina.

But some have questioned whether the recent snafus signal that Jeffries and other leaders may not be ready to be in command of the House majority.

"I may have to rethink my support of Hakeem Jeffries after the Hegseth impeachment vote," Fred Trump III, a Democrat, author and nephew of President Donald Trump, posted on X. "Eleven Democrats do not show up? All Republicans vote it down."

"Pete Hegseth is laughing at you and is stronger today. Shame," he continued. "A slap in the face of the military and veterans on this important day."

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks alongside Rep. Pete Aguilar and Rep. Katherine Clark during a news conference in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 8, 2026. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

HEGSETH THWARTS GOP-LED IMPEACHMENT PUSH AS QUESTIONS SWIRL OVER WHETHER ALLEGATIONS RISE TO HIGH CRIMES

House GOP leaders successfully blocked Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., from leading the charge to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth earlier this week.

Part of the reason for the failure was the absence of 11 House Democrats during a procedural vote on Tuesday evening.

Had just seven of them been present, the vote to kill Massie's impeachment resolution would have failed, triggering debate and a vote on impeaching the Cabinet secretary likely the next day.

"Everyone knew that attendance was key tonight but somehow Democratic leaders failed to deliver and handed Republicans a win," Demand Progress Executive Director Sean Vitka said in a statement.

'THE VIEW' CO-HOST CALLS DEMOCRATS MISSING HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT VOTE A 'SELF-INFLICTED WOUND'

Progressive journalist David Schuster wrote on X, "Sure, house Dems will have 259 seats in January instead of current 213. And Hegseth impeachment can be reintroduced. But Hakeem having 11 Dem absences today on Hegseth (thus losing vote) reveals a Hakeem leadership problem. Embarrassing."

An emotional Rep. Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., said in a video posted to X that she and other Democrats were stuck in traffic when they missed the vote.

Various reports, however, said they were at a fundraiser less than two miles from the U.S. Capitol.

U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth takes questions from reporters during a news conference at the Pentagon on Nov. 10, 2026, in Arlington, Va. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

HOUSE DEM MISSES HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT VOTE BECAUSE OF MAJOR MEDICAL PROCEDURE ONE WEEK AFTER ELECTION DAY

Others blamed medical procedures and family emergencies.

The day after, a bill Democratic leadership was actively urging lawmakers to vote against passed by unanimous voice vote — simply because no Democrats called for a roll call instead.

Democrats accused Republicans of parliamentary tricks, including a post on the X account belonging to the House Veterans Affairs Committee minority, "Republicans pushed it through that way intentionally so their members wouldn’t have to go on the record supporting cuts to veterans’ benefits."

But the majority of Democrats do not believe it is an early blight on Jeffries' potential speakership.

HAKEEM JEFFRIES DECLARES BID FOR HOUSE SPEAKER AFTER GOP'S MIDTERM MASSACRE

"I think there's frustration in terms of whipping votes. I'm not entirely sure where the breakdown is.  And it does seem like there's maybe some tension somewhere," Democratic strategist Mike Nellis told Fox News Digital. "I think it'll be incumbent on the incoming speaker to make sure that everybody feels like they're on the same page ... beyond that, if you're asking me if it makes a difference in a leadership flight, I mean, nobody's running against Hakeem. I haven't heard of anybody seriously thinking about doing that, so I don't know that it'll change anything."

He said House Democrats largely "have faith" in Jeffries and House Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., who is poised to be the next House Majority Leader.

Democrat Dan Turrentine, co-host of "The Huddle," told Fox News Digital "a few Democrats unintentionally missed one vote. Unfortunately, this happens periodically in both chambers, for both parties. It does not speak to Jeffries' leadership."

And other House Democrats, when asked, directed frustration at their colleagues instead.

Rep. Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., arrives for the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee deposition of former Attorney General Pam Bondi about the Jeffrey Epstein files, in the Rayburn building on Friday, May 29, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"My message is always to members that we need to be here and be on time," Clark told reporters Wednesday. "But there was a clear message from the Republican Party as well that they are unwilling, even after this election, to stand up against Hegseth in this war."

Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., said, "It's unfortunate, but that's not on leadership."

Fox News Digital reached out to Jeffries' political team for comment.

#5954. The True Meaning of Power

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

What the Godfather of Realism Can Teach Trump

“International politics, like all politics, is a struggle for power.” Hans Morgenthau wrote this sentence from his desk in Chicago at the dawn of the Cold War, as the United States and the Soviet Union embarked on an open-ended competition for global dominance. Politics Among Nations, the volume that Morgenthau ultimately produced, would quickly become the most widely adopted international relations textbook in the United States and provide an intellectual framework—realism—that would guide generations of scholars and policymakers.

Although much has changed in the nearly eight decades since Morgenthau’s most influential work was published, the fundamentals remain the same. Human nature, which for Morgenthau drove the struggle for power, is unmoved. States are still the most significant actors in the international system and compete for influence. Great powers continue to drive the course of history. Much of today’s world would seem to affirm Morgenthau’s conclusions: Russia’s attempts to establish a sphere of influence in Eastern Europe, China’s quest for hegemony in East Asia, and the United States’ revival of the Monroe Doctrine in the Western Hemisphere all suggest the enduring primacy of national interests over moral aspirations and international norms.

For many, Morgenthau’s contributions begin and end with his identification of power as the key determinant of state behavior. But this reading misses one of his core observations: that even if humans tend to be power-maximizing creatures, they are also moral beings who seek to limit their own power. Morgenthau’s writings reveal a dialectic between power and morality—two seemingly incompatible concepts that he spent his life attempting to reconcile. Far from romanticizing power, Morgenthau saw the need to tame it.

An immigrant who escaped Nazi Germany and owed his life to the United States, Morgenthau had specific guidance to offer his fellow Americans. Even as he urged the United States to protect its vital interests by maintaining a favorable balance of power in key regions, he implored the country to wield its power prudently. Morgenthau saw the United States as the only country with both the capacity and the will to fight on behalf of transcendent values that he believed power had to serve. He was committed to preserving American power as a check on the violence and bigotry he experienced. Yet he feared that U.S. overreach would hollow out the foundations of that power. This, for Morgenthau, would be a tragedy for humanity.

Perhaps no government has misread Morgenthau more than the second Trump administration. Its officials revel in the exercise of military force around the world, from Iran to Venezuela and the Caribbean, while dismissing concerns of alleged war crimes and threatening long-standing allies. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller typified the Trumpian outlook when, in January, he invoked the “iron laws of the world,” one “governed by strength,” “governed by force,” and “governed by power.”

Some analysts have also erroneously rooted the Trump administration’s actions in realism. A lengthy essay in The New York Times Magazine, for instance, ran under the headline “The Theory That Gives Trump a Blank Check for Aggression.” This is understandable, as the Trump administration has repeatedly claimed its actions are underpinned by “flexible realism.”

But any reading of realism that does not consider the moral dimensions of Morgenthau’s theory is both mistaken and dangerous. When the United States limits its own power, abiding by international norms, consulting allies and partners, and wielding its strength in pursuit of transcendent values, countries find American influence more palatable, which helps sustain it. But if Washington’s actions become untethered from these restraints, others will no longer defer to American prerogatives, and the world will become a more dangerous place.

Returning to the foundations of realism—to the man who introduced this intellectual tradition to Americans—is critical. If Morgenthau were to witness this moment in U.S. history, he would conclude that the country had overlearned his lessons about the importance of power and erred in equating it with the use of force. He would see a need to elevate moral questions and rebuild normative constraints on the exercise of power. And he would warn against foreign entanglements that undermine American democracy, which remains the wellspring of the country’s power. These are the lessons that will help the United States navigate an era of intensified great-power competition, one in which the margin for error is thin and the cost of miscalculation could be catastrophic.

Morgenthau was born into an assimilated, middle-class Jewish family in southern Germany in the winter of 1904. His conservative and authoritarian father, Ludwig, raised his only child to revere the monarchy and take pride in their country’s achievements. Morgenthau’s childhood might have passed as that of a shy, precocious boy in a self-assured bourgeois community, but Germany’s defeat in World War I and the rise of anti-Semitism set his life on a drastically different course.

In 1922, as a top student in his high school, Morgenthau was chosen to address his classmates and neighbors in a public ceremony honoring the school’s namesake. When he began to speak, he noticed that some had turned their backs and others were holding their noses at this “stinking Jew.” Morgenthau finished his remarks, but as he left the square, his classmates hurled anti-Semitic insults and spat on him. Just months later, Hitler descended on Morgenthau’s hometown of Coburg with hundreds of storm troopers, who assaulted protesters while the police looked on. Coburg soon gained the ignominious distinction of being the first town to elect the Nazis to power.

Morgenthau left Coburg hoping to become a writer or poet but was forced to pivot to law after hyperinflation ruined his family’s finances. During his apprenticeship under Hugo Sinzheimer, a leading left-wing labor lawyer, he saw conservative judges undermine the Weimar Republic and aid those who sought its destruction. Morgenthau later reflected in his intellectual autobiography that this led him to conclude that “what was decisive was not the merits of different legal interpretations but the distribution of political power.”

As life for German Jews deteriorated, he fled to Geneva to teach law. Switzerland was unfortunately not far enough away; after Hitler took power in Germany, students began boycotting his classes because they did not want to learn German law from a Jew. He then found a teaching position in Madrid but was displaced by the Spanish Civil War and wandered through Europe before arriving in New York in 1937 as a penniless refugee. Having witnessed the rise of fascism up close, Morgenthau was shocked to find that so many Americans believed that human nature was fundamentally good, that peace was the normal condition of humanity, and that history was a story of progress.

In New York and then Kansas City, Morgenthau grew alarmed as the United States watched Nazi Germany rearm, annex Austria, and invade Czechoslovakia. He believed that a failure to understand human nature had inspired Western democracies’ blind faith in international law and the League of Nations, leading them down the path of least resistance with appeasement of Hitler, straight into the moral abyss.

Shaken by the fall of France in 1940, Morgenthau began writing his first English-language book, taking aim at Americans’ confidence that the methods of the natural sciences could make sense of the social world and that the sheer force of reason would eventually eliminate conflict. In Scientific Man vs. Power Politics, published in 1946, he charged that rationalism and liberalism had misunderstood the nature of man, the nature of the world, and the nature of reason itself. Humans, in addition to having rational needs, possessed irrational impulses that could not be reasoned away. Man’s “lust for power would be satisfied only … if he became like God.” Countries, like humans, sought to maximize their power over one another, making conflict inevitable.

Scientific Man received disastrous reviews, and Morgenthau later recalled that it “shocked people to no end.” He adjusted his approach, tailoring his message to Americans and packaging it in a textbook that would appeal to their pragmatism. He wanted this book to mark an evolution in American thinking about foreign policy, privately writing that it would differ from its predecessors “as an automobile differs from a horse and buggy.” Two years later, in Politics Among Nations, he achieved that goal. Morgenthau stressed that the struggle for power was inescapable. All states sought to keep, increase, or demonstrate their strength. Disarmament, collective security, and international law would not contain this struggle. Only a balance of power could prevent countries from attempting to overthrow the existing order. Power could be tamed only by countervailing power.

It is easy to see why many misread Morgenthau as a champion of realpolitik—an heir to the likes of Machiavelli or Bismarck. After all, he placed power at the center of his analysis. But he never romanticized it. As he wrote in a private letter, “I am an analyst of the nation state and of power and have emphasized time and again their negative moral connotations.” Morgenthau’s personal encounters with power had taught him that its unbridled pursuit led to calamity. He understood that normative and moral limitations were required to keep the struggle for power within tolerable bounds. As he wrote in another letter, “It is the task of civilized societies to temper the power drives and direct them into socially useful channels.”

Indeed, Morgenthau had less tolerance for those who failed to reconcile power with morality than for those who underestimated power’s importance. Although President Woodrow Wilson’s universalism and idealism made him one of Morgenthau’s favorite targets, he preferred him to a Machiavellian prince: “Wilson’s failure was at least the failure of greatness, of too great a vision. Nobody will say as much for the epigones of Machiavelli.” He similarly criticized the British historian and political theorist E. H. Carr, whose moral relativism had led him to advocate for appeasing Hitler. Carr, he wrote, had “no transcendent point of view from which to survey the political scene and to appraise the phenomenon of power.” While both men are seen as pivotal realist thinkers, Morgenthau witheringly concluded of Carr that “it is a dangerous thing to be a Machiavelli. It is a disastrous thing to be a Machiavelli without virtù”—that is, it is ruinous to practice power politics without skill and judgment.

In Politics Among Nations, Morgenthau took issue with leaders who both glorify the struggle for power and reject any limits on their own use of power. He argued that “philosophies and political systems which have made the lust and the struggle for power their mainstay have proved impotent and self-destructive.” And he drew attention to common moral standards that could sustain order and moderate the struggle for power. He observed that throughout history, humans insisted on subjecting political action to ethical scrutiny. When such restraints held, countries did less than their power enabled them to do; once commonplace practices, such as assassinating a rival country’s leaders or killing a large portion of its civilian population to reduce its strength, became stigmatized. Morgenthau concluded, “What has changed is the influence of civilization which makes what is desirable and feasible ethically reprehensible and, hence, normally impossible of execution.”

In the immediate aftermath of World War II, however, he believed that the limitations on the struggle for power had reached their weakest point since the advent of the modern state system. Hitler had attempted to extinguish a whole people, and both the Axis and the Allied powers had bombed cities indiscriminately. Although Morgenthau believed the Allies were morally justified in taking such actions to defeat a genocidal regime, he nonetheless feared that the struggle for power was on its way to becoming boundless. In the nuclear age, failing to reestablish these moral barriers could mean the end of humanity.

Morgenthau’s hard-nosed reputation has long obscured the moral core of his realism. He was unequivocal that power must be a means to an end—“an attempt to realize moral values through the medium of politics.” He recognized that maximizing power for its own sake was both destructive and pointless, arguing that “a nation must pursue its interests for the sake of a transcendent purpose which gives meaning to the day-to-day operations of its foreign policy.” In his view, ancient Greece and Rome are remembered because their power served a purpose that outlived their empires: Athenian democracy and philosophy, and Roman law and republican government.

As he assimilated and raised a family in Chicago, Morgenthau came to see the United States as the inheritor of this tradition. The country’s contribution to the world and the source of its power lay in its democracy and civic life. A realist approach—one that prudently wielded power abroad—was best suited to protect the American experiment at home, enabling Americans to live in freedom and security while offering an example for other countries to emulate. In other words, American power had to be bound to purpose—a purpose the country fulfilled “as a light to attract strangers, not as a flame to be spread throughout the world.” This was not merely the observation of a dispassionate scholar. The United States had accepted Morgenthau when no other country would, and it was a place where immigrants like him could rise to the top of their fields.

By the 1960s, Morgenthau saw that American power faced a threat of its own making. He began to develop deep misgivings about U.S. intervention in Vietnam, warning as early as 1961 that it could become a quagmire reminiscent of France’s war in Algeria. Two years later, as clashes between the South Vietnamese government and protesters intensified, Morgenthau urged the United States to get out. He built his opposition on realist grounds, arguing that a communist takeover of Vietnam would not affect the balance of power in Asia, thus rejecting the domino theory, which held that communism would spread inexorably outward once it gained a regional foothold. Morgenthau also recognized that communism was no longer monolithic and believed that Ho Chi Minh could lead a nonaligned country as Tito did in Yugoslavia. He saw the conflict as a civil war and worried that the United States was attempting to maintain a status quo that was itself the source of instability.

Successive administrations failed to heed Morgenthau’s warnings and instead plunged the United States deeper into the war. He came to resent American policymakers’ misappropriation of his lessons on power and entered public debate with new vigor. At a packed rally in New York’s Madison Square Garden in June 1965, he warned that a guerrilla war could be won only through the indiscriminate killing of the South Vietnamese people, which would tear at the moral fiber of the United States. Later that month, Morgenthau debated President Lyndon Johnson’s national security adviser, McGeorge Bundy, on national television. He led with his moral outrage: “I am opposed to our present policy in Vietnam on moral, military, political, and general intellectual grounds.”

The greatest risk of the war, Morgenthau discerned, was “the risk to ourselves, to our mission in the world, to our very existence as a distinct nation.” He lamented, “Here is the last best hope of the downtrodden and the enslaved, to which men of good will throughout the world have looked as a shining example, relieving its frustration in blind ideological fury and aimless destructiveness upon a helpless people.” Vietnam, in his telling, had corrupted the very purpose that gave American power its meaning.

The Vietnam War validated Morgenthau’s belief that power untethered from questions of morality would lead to overreach. It proved that the United States had an interest in constraining itself, if only to avoid disaster. More fundamentally, Vietnam showed that misadventures abroad could boomerang, weakening American democracy and societal cohesion and, ultimately, undermining the country’s international standing.

The second Trump administration’s foreign policy record has thrown these insights into sharp relief. Its officials view questions of morality as a costly sideshow, the remit of woolly-minded idealists who do not understand how the world works. The White House has time and again resorted to military force, striking boats in the Caribbean, kidnapping Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, blockading Cuba, and waging war on Iran. It has also threatened military action against Canada and Denmark, two of the country’s long-standing allies.

American democracy, far from serving as “a light to attract strangers,” is fast becoming a cautionary tale. The second Trump administration has undermined the foundations of American power through attacks on the courts, the press, and universities. It has gleefully bulldozed through any checks on its writ. Its assault on institutions and its aggressive foreign policy are intertwined; the administration not only failed to seek congressional authorization for the war in Iran, but it also refused to even make the case to the American people before striking.

President Donald Trump has justified his aggression on the basis of the “iron laws that have always determined global power.” Morgenthau would not have recognized this as realism. He contended that “superior power gives no right, either moral or legal, to do with that power all that it is physically capable of doing.” The Trump administration, by contrast, seems to believe that to not use the power at its disposal is to waste it. Morgenthau’s verdict on Carr applies equally to Trump: he is a “Machiavelli without virtù,” playing power politics without judgment and leading his country to disaster.

Morgenthau would argue that the Trump administration misunderstands the very concept of power, which should not be equated with military might and must instead be understood as a complex psychological relationship. Real power, Morgenthau insisted, lies in the ability to influence a country through consent, not coercion. In this view, the use of force signifies the abdication of political power rather than its culmination. The Trump administration’s belligerence betrays its weakness: its acts of aggression around the world are confessions of its inability to shape events through other means.

Although Morgenthau grew up on the statecraft of Bismarck, he came to admire Abraham Lincoln above all others, even attempting to write a book about him toward the end of his life. Morgenthau saw in Lincoln a rare leader who was never possessed by power, instead possessing it and, ultimately, subordinating it to transcendent values. Today, just as at the height of the Vietnam War, Morgenthau would see his task as restoring morality and ethics to their rightful place and highlighting the need for power to move the world toward justice.

The United States has lost its purpose, and unless it rediscovers it, discrete foreign policy successes will be irrelevant. As Morgenthau wrote, if the country loses its soul, any victories are merely “footnotes to the history of the decline and fall of a once great nation.”

DAVID SACKS is Senior Fellow for Asia Studies at the Council on Foreign Relations and the author of the forthcoming book The Realist: Hans Morgenthau and the Purpose of American Power.

#5953. Huang Out at Nvidia

World Brief: Huang Out at Nvidia

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Europe’s future involvement in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and mounting political tensions in Indonesia.

Two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, marked the undoing of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday amid growing calls for his departure and a substantial drop in the company’s stock price.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Europe’s future involvement in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and mounting political tensions in Indonesia.

Two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, marked the undoing of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday amid growing calls for his departure and a substantial drop in the company’s stock price.

Huang has been seen as the face of the global artificial intelligence race. His company is the world’s leading producer of advanced semiconductor chips, making Nvidia a critical part of U.S. national security and a sought-after partner of China. Huang himself is among the world’s wealthiest people, with an estimated net worth of around $162 billion prior to his recent scandal.

Over the past two years, Huang has also become a close friend of U.S. President Donald Trump, whose administration has made advancing AI a cornerstone of its agenda. Notably, Huang successfully petitioned the White House last December to relax some restrictions on Nvidia sales to China in exchange for the U.S. government receiving a 25 percent cut of the profits.

But in just two weeks, Huang’s public image has collapsed. Late last month, the New York Times reported that a Chinese businesswoman believed to be spying for Beijing was in a “close relationship” with Huang. The alleged spy, Alice Huang, was an executive at a Singapore-based data center company, Megaspeed, which the U.S. Commerce Department began suspecting in 2024 of helping China to smuggle in Nvidia’s restricted AI chips.

Nvidia shares plummeted in the wake of the news, even as Beijing denied involvement. Huang admitted to the affair in an email to Nvidia’s 42,000-plus employees on Sunday.

However, the scandal didn’t end there. On Wednesday, the Times reported that Huang had had a separate affair with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare. That relationship may have violated the company’s code of conduct. Huang has not publicly acknowledged the second affair.

The dual allegations appear to have been enough to force Huang to step down. Huang has reportedly agreed to testify before Congress ahead of the U.S. holiday of Thanksgiving over the espionage scandal. And Nvidia finance chief Colette Kress has agreed to serve as interim CEO until a replacement is named.

Nvidia’s change in leadership, though, has yet to assuage global markets. Company shares plunged as much as 14 percent when trading opened on Thursday, extending a crisis that has already wiped out more than $1 trillion from Nvidia’s market value. Some initial gains were made later in the day but not enough to reverse the damage.

Nvidia’s board has said there is “no reason to believe” that Huang’s actions compromised U.S. national security or company secrets, but it has launched an independent investigation. And on Thursday, Megaspeed CEO Tan Yong Pong issued a statement saying that the company takes its obligation to comply with U.S. export control laws “extremely seriously” and will work “constructively and transparently with the U.S. government.”

Trump, meanwhile, praised Huang on Thursday, writing on Truth Social that he had done a “fantastic job” with Nvidia.

A seat at the table. Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed on Thursday to allow European representatives to join the next round of direct Ukraine peace talks. Giving Europe a seat at the table marks a big win for Kyiv and Washington, which have both pushed for greater European involvement in negotiations. However, the concession could also spell trouble for future talks, as Moscow remains largely at odds with its European counterparts.

“We would very much like you, gentlemen, and the U.S. administration as a whole to work with your European allies so that they can finally make up their minds as to what they want: peace or war in Ukraine,” Putin told U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow on Thursday. At the same time, the Russian leader warned that any push for the deployment of European troops to Ukraine after a peace deal is inked would trigger renewed fighting.

Witkoff and Kushner will now head to Dublin for similar talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. The potential of European involvement in the peace process will almost certainly be on the agenda, but Zelensky is also likely to bring up new reports of Starlink disruptions in Ukraine.

Zelensky on Thursday accused the U.S.-based company of placing speed restrictions on its Starshield military-grade services, affecting how its drone interceptors operate. The last time that such limits were detected, Zelensky resumed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries in direct opposition to Trump’s wishes. Kyiv and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had both accused the Trump administration of orchestrating that incident, which the White House denied.

Academic scandal. Indonesian Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka submitted his resignation to parliament on Thursday in the wake of a scandal over his academic credentials. It is unclear when his departure will take effect; however, experts expect the incident to deliver another blow to the tenuous alliance between former President Joko “Jokowi” Widodo and current President Prabowo Subianto.

Calls for Gibran’s impeachment first intensified last month, when the country’s Constitutional Court found that the vice president did not possess the necessary credentials to hold power. In Indonesia, lawmakers must have a high school diploma to run for office. Gibran claimed to have finished grade 12 at a school in Australia, but the court ruled that the degree was not equivalent to an Indonesian senior high school certificate. Two weeks later, the country’s Supreme Court backed that ruling by revoking Gibran’s equivalency document.

Gibran was elected in 2024 largely as a symbol of the precarious truce between his father, Jokowi, and Prabowo. His removal could therefore further fracture that fragile alliance. Just last week, Indonesian authorities detained three senior police officials suspected of wiretapping the president and dozens of other prominent figures. Among those arrested was Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who was a known loyalist of Jokowi.

Gaza hospital attack. An Israeli airstrike targeted the main hospital in the southern Gaza city of Khan Younis overnight on Thursday, killing at least six people, including a teenager, and injuring at least 20 others. Locals reported two missiles damaging a building containing surgical wards at Nasser Hospital. The attack marked the latest violation of the region’s precarious Gaza cease-fire, which took effect in October 2025.

According to Israel’s military, the hospital strike was part of an operation targeting Muhammad Abu Ismail, whom Israeli forces described as the “commander of Hamas’s Khan Younis Brigade.” Israel claimed that Abu Ismail had turned Nasser Hospital into his headquarters and was using the facility as a base of operations. Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of using civilian infrastructure as human shields. The militant group has denied doing so.

Since the Israel-Hamas war began in October 2023, Israeli troops have attacked Nasser Hospital at least seven times, according to hospital officials. The use of medical centers for military purposes and the targeting of such sites are both considered violations of international law. “Gaza’s health facilities are lifelines for its ​people,” World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote on X on Thursday. “They must be protected. They must never be militarized or attacked.”

The Finnish Embassy in Canberra temporarily closed its doors on Tuesday for a one-day internal planning and staff sauna event. However, what was meant to be a routine disruption instead appeared to upend the internet, with a deluge of memes jokingly bemoaning the closure. Local swimming pools offered their services for those suffering, a Dutch esports league complained about the lockout, and even American Airlines unveiled a snap sale on flights to Europe for emotional support.

The embassy, meanwhile, took the public’s outcry in stride. “After 24 harrowing hours, international expressions of grief and an unprecedented outpouring of solidarity, the Embassy of Finland in Canberra has officially reopened,” the facility posted on social media on Wednesday, marking the event with a ribbon-cutting ceremony.

Alexandra Sharp is the World Brief writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @alexandrassharp.bsky.social X: @AlexandraSSharp

#5952. Rubio’s next move? Lawyers eye speech of 'visionary' leader for 2028 clues after GOP’s midterm wipeout

Federalist Society convention attendees weigh whether Rubio will offer a Republican roadmap to recovery, defend the administration’s foreign policy or signal his own political ambitions.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio will deliver his first major speech apart from his diplomatic duties Friday following the GOP’s blowout midterm losses, with some attendees at the Federalist Society's National Lawyers Convention eager to hear how he will chart a path forward as the 2028 presidential race draws closer.

"I think it will be an interesting speech to see what he says post midterms," attendee Isaiah McKinney told Fox News Digital. "I'm expecting him to discuss both the successes and failures of the administration and what his plans are moving forward — especially as the secretary of state. I hope he addresses the foreign policy implications and how he thinks foreign policy played a role into that, into the election results."

Rubio will deliver an approximately 45-minute speech for the Barbara Olson Memorial Lecture, whose previous speakers include former Attorney General Bill Barr and The Free Press founder Bari Weiss.

But another question weighs heavily on the minds of attendees at the annual conference in Washington, D.C., which attracts prominent lawyers affiliated with the conservative movement.

HOUSE CONSERVATIVE EMERGES WITH 2028 PRESIDENTIAL PICK AFTER GOP'S MIDTERM MASSACRE: 'I AM ALL IN'

Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks to the media before departing from Homestead Air Reserve Base in Homestead, Florida, on November 8, 2026, ahead of his journey to France for the G7 Foreign Ministers' Meeting. (Brendan Smialowski/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

"There are a lot of people in the room who are going to be wondering if he's still planning on running for president someday," Rachel Paulose, a former U.S. attorney and general counsel at Upper Midwest Law Center, told Fox News Digital. "That will be a question that will be top of mind for a lot of people."

The question comes following a CNN report citing officials close to Vice President JD Vance — often described as President Donald Trump's MAGA heir apparent — who expressed concern that Republicans would not be able to win the 2028 presidential race if the Iran war remains an issue during the campaign.

Republicans lost a net 41 House seats and eight Senate seats, with Alaska's Senate race still undecided, marking the largest simultaneous loss in both chambers of Congress for Republicans in a midterm election since 1958. President Donald Trump has partly blamed the losses on voters' opposition to the Iran war, and Vance was more direct about the war's impact on the election results, though Rubio has yet to weigh in.

"The fact of the matter is that the Republicans got blown out pretty well in the recent election," John Shu, a legal commentator who served in the administrations of former Presidents George H. W. Bush and George W. Bush, told Fox News Digital. "And it's possible that he may talk about the budgetary process. It'll be interesting to see what the Democratic House and the Democrat Senate will do regarding funding of the State Department."

Shu said Rubio could also address U. S. strikes on suspected drug cartels off the coast of Venezuela in fall 2025, which drew sharp criticism from Democratic lawmakers, including six Democrats with military or intelligence backgrounds who released a video urging service members to disobey unlawful orders.

CONSERVATIVES STUNNED BY 'CATASTROPHIC' MIDTERM BLUE TSUNAMI, BLAME TRUMP'S IRAN WAR, HIGH GAS PRICES

Vice President JD Vance, left, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are viewed by many Republicans as potential 2028 presidential contenders. (Annabelle Gordon/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Kylie Cooper/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

"I don't know that he's going to address the domestic policies. I mean, he's the secretary of state," Shu said.

Trump has previously floated a 2028 ticket pairing Vance and Rubio, who at one point held four senior administration roles simultaneously and became the subject of a running internet joke about his expanding portfolio. Trump has also joked about who would top the ticket.

"I don't know anything about who's going to run in 2028, but what I appreciate about Secretary Rubio is he is traveling all around the country and all around the world to talk about the importance of American values, what binds us, what brings us all together, and the importance of our Constitution," Iowa Solicitor General Eric Wessan told Fox News Digital.

TRUMP TOLD DONORS 'WE NEED TO ELECT JD,' SOURCE CONFIRMS, AS HE WEIGHS VANCE OR RUBIO IN 2028

Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks during a Cabinet meeting at the White House on Dec. 2, 2025, in Washington. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Rubio’s address at the Mayflower Hotel follows a trip to Paris this week for G-7 meetings focused on Iran, Ukraine and other international challenges.

"I think that Secretary Rubio already is a person of high standing for a lot of people in this room," Paulose told Fox News Digital.

RUBIO SOUNDS CAMPAIGN-READY AS HE RAILS AGAINST OPEN BORDERS, GLOBALISM IN SPEECH FROM ANCIENT GREEK RUINS

Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants, was first elected to the U. S. Senate representing Florida in 2010, and served until 2025, when Trump tapped him to become secretary of state.

Rubio ran for president in 2016, dropping out of the race after losing his home-state primary in Florida.

"There are people who have worked for him, who've campaigned for him, who've believed in him for a very long time and who've seen him at his best, but I also think that there's a real opportunity for him to deliver a positive message and a path forward for the movement," Paulose told Fox News Digital.

Fox News Digital reached out to the State Department and the White House for comment but did not receive a response before publication.

Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

#5950. Hegseth’s Troubles Are Far From Over

Situation Report: Hegseth’s Troubles Are Far From Over

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report. It’s been a wild week of news, and our heads are still spinning. We’ve got a very full edition for you this week.

Here’s what’s on tap for the day: Hegseth escapes impeachment for the time being, Russia’s ambassador to Washington dies, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report. It’s been a wild week of news, and our heads are still spinning. We’ve got a very full edition for you this week.

Here’s what’s on tap for the day: Hegseth escapes impeachment for the time being, Russia’s ambassador to Washington dies, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns.

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth narrowly escaped an impeachment effort this week, but questions remain over his job security.

The push to impeach Hegseth, led by outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, was blocked by Republicans in the House on Tuesday. The House voted 211 to 204 on a motion to refer the articles of impeachment to the House Judiciary Committee, which effectively tanked the chances of Hegseth getting impeached—for now. Eleven Democrats missed the vote, which helped House Republicans pass the motion by seven votes.

But Hegseth’s troubles are far from over as Republicans continue to contend with the fallout from their disastrous performance in the midterms, which was driven in part by voter discontent over the economic consequences of the Iran war. In Washington, Hegseth is seen as the face of that war, as well as other controversial military actions that President Donald Trump has taken in Latin America, putting the defense secretary’s future in question as the political landscape shifts.

What’s next for Hegseth. Democrats could launch another effort to impeach Hegseth in a new Congress. “This is not the end of it. It’s just the beginning,” Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to be the next House speaker, said after the impeachment vote this week.

Democrats will have the votes in the House to impeach Hegseth in a new Congress. But they’re less likely to garner the support of enough Republicans in the Senate to convict and remove the defense secretary.

Whether Democrats pursue impeachment or not, Hegseth will be under a microscope. Democrats have been clear that they will leverage their oversight powers to investigate him on everything from the Iran war and the military operation that led to the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro to the lethal strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats near Latin America. Even some Republicans in recent days have suggested that he should just resign and said that they want more answers on the Iran war.

Trump has backed Hegseth so far and signaled that he doesn’t plan to fire him. As long as the president stands by him, Hegseth might be able to save his job. People have been “predicting that Secretary Hegseth would be on his way out” since the Signalgate controversy, said Peter Feaver, a professor of political science and public policy at Duke University.

“He’s shown that he’s quite adept at holding on to his position because he’s maintained the confidence of the one person that matters in the administration, and that’s President Trump,” Feaver said. “I don’t see evidence that he has lost President Trump’s confidence. If anything, Trump is more fulsome in his expressions of support for Secretary Hegseth.”

Hegseth vs. Congress. Hegseth, a former Fox News host, went on the offensive in the past week, launching a campaign-style media blitz against his opponents in Congress, posting about it on social media, and delivering a fiery speech at a rare press conference from the Pentagon. It was indicative of the unusually partisan approach that Hegseth has taken to his role. Some watchdogs have also suggested that Hegseth’s messaging campaign violated federal law.

Defense secretaries are meant to be political animals who are “very nonpartisan” but “really wily at working Congress,” Feaver said. “Hegseth has not fit that mold,” Feaver added, describing him as the “most partisan” defense secretary in modern times. While this has helped Hegseth maintain Trump’s trust, the defense secretary “also answers to Congress,” Feaver said, especially when it comes to the defense budget that the Defense Department relies on.

The National Defense Authorization Act, the annual defense policy bill that dictates yearly U.S. military spending levels, is stalled in Congress. The White House has been pressing Congress to pass a record budget request of $1.5 trillion, but Hegseth’s recent attack campaign may have made this even harder than it already was in a lame-duck session.

It also doesn’t set the Pentagon up “for success in the last two years in terms of working with the new Congress,” Feaver said. Trump on Thursday called on Senate Republicans to “IMMEDIATELY” pass $350 billion in defense spending via reconciliation before Democrats take over.

Hegseth is used to a less active Congress, but that’s about to change with Democrats at the helm. “There’s a saying in the military—you don’t fight against the terrain,” Feaver said.

Russian Ambassador to the United States Alexander Darchiev died aged 66 in Moscow, the Russian Foreign Ministry announced on Wednesday. Darchiev had been posted in Washington since March 2025 but returned to Moscow to seek treatment for a chronic illness, CNN reported.

Erik Slavin, the former editor in chief of the Pentagon-funded newspaper Stars and Stripes, announced on Wednesday that he would be joining the Atlantic as a staff writer covering the U.S. military. Slavin was fired from his post at Stars and Stripes in August for alleged insubordination after he defended the publication’s editorial independence.

What should be high on your radar, if it isn’t already.

Russia-Ukraine stalemate continues. Trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine, and the United States held in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, failed to yield a major breakthrough this week, save for an agreement for Russia and Ukraine to exchange prisoners of war. The broader sticking points that have dogged the conflict remain, including the prospect of a temporary cease-fire and both sides’ territorial claims on the front lines.

The Kremlin appears unwilling to cede any ground, with lead Russian negotiator Vladimir Medinsky telling reporters after the talks that “every square foot of land will be returned to Russia one way or another.” U.S. negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday before heading to Dublin for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that same day. Witkoff told reporters in Moscow that European officials will join the next round of talks—a potentially significant step given that Putin has long resisted any European role in talks to end the war.

Vance reassigned. Trump announced in a Truth Social post on Thursday that he has ordered Vice President J.D. Vance “to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.” instead of working on negotiations with Iran. Vance has been leading those negotiations and was reportedly set to meet with a senior Iranian security official to try to end the war.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!,” Trump wrote.

As John reported, Vance last week blamed the Iran war for Republicans’ midterm losses in a rare public statement.

Huang’s out. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday—the latest twist in a weekslong scandal that has unleashed turmoil at the $4 trillion company whose semiconductor chips have become indispensable to the development of artificial intelligence. Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy and is accused of having another one with a subordinate at Nvidia.

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, has overseen the company’s rise into a technology behemoth and has himself become the face of the global AI race. His departure has implications far beyond the company or any one country. Rishi explains why in his piece on the saga.

Pro-Palestinian protesters attend a rally at Trinity College in Dublin, Ireland, on Nov. 10 during a visit by former U.S. President Joe Biden.Li Mangmang/Xinhua via Getty Images

Monday, Nov. 16: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit begins in Manila, Philippines, with the group hosting bilateral summits with China, Australia, and South Korea.

Tuesday, Nov. 17: Trump arrives in Manila for the ASEAN-U.S. special summit and Quad leaders summit.

Wednesday, Nov. 18: The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation economic leaders meeting begins in Shenzhen, China.

Thursday, Nov. 19: The International Court of Justice is scheduled to pronounce its final judgment on accusations of genocide against Myanmar over its campaign against Rohingya Muslims.

Friday, Nov. 20: The European Union hosts the EU-U.K. summit.

50—the number of ballistic missiles that Iran continues to produce every month, according to Western intelligence estimates cited by Bloomberg.

“My analogy would be … the Titanic hit the iceberg on Nov. 3, and I came up with a life raft, and they said, ‘No thanks, we’re going to stick on the Titanic.’”

—Massie to MS NOW after his motion to impeach Hegseth failed in the House.

#5948. Democrats Shouldn’t Squander Their Chance to Launch a Foreign Policy Revolution

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

MATTHEW DUSS is Executive Vice President of the Center for International Policy. From 2017 to 2022, he served as Chief Foreign Policy Adviser to Senator Bernie Sanders.

The Imperative of Ambition in a New Congress

Tuesday’s election made clear that endless wars, political corruption, and the high cost of living are three of the American public’s top concerns. They are deeply interrelated—and the new Congress must address all three. That will require a true foreign policy revolution that grapples not just with the outrages and failures of the Trump administration’s foreign policy but also with the ways in which past Democratic or Democrat-supported foreign policies have contributed to today’s crisis. There will be a temptation among some Democratic leaders, in Congress and beyond, to limit the scope or pace of change. But to find a way out of today’s crisis and move beyond the failures that have afflicted American foreign policy for the past several decades, Democrats will need to have the courage to face a hard truth: that President Donald Trump’s abuses of power and unilateral warmaking are not so much a break from Washington’s militarist mindset as they are a particularly aggressive, predatory expression of it.

The incoming Democratic majority will face a national security environment in which the most severe challenges to U.S. safety and prosperity come from within. That’s why Congress should shut down the Iran war immediately but also recognize that it can make the United States more secure only if it pairs a foreign policy shift with a frontal assault on spiraling costs and political corruption. Political polarization; government corruption and dysfunction; increasing dominance of political and economic life by a small handful of mercurial oligarchs; and a president who recklessly and unilaterally launches unauthorized military interventions while relentlessly seeking opportunities to enrich himself, his family, and his cronies—all pose more immediate danger to the safety and prosperity of the American people than does any foreign enemy.

When Democrats take control of Congress in January, they will have considerable power to challenge the corruption and malfeasance of the Trump administration. Control of committees and of the congressional calendar will provide the opportunity for sorely needed oversight. But although the Trump administration deserves aggressive investigation, Democrats must aim higher—and use the opportunity to articulate a genuinely compelling alternative for American foreign policy.

The first and most urgent task will be ending the Iran war, a reckless and unpopular conflict that has become even less popular as Americans have felt its effects on their wallets. Congress must respond to widespread bipartisan anger among voters at Trump’s war and abuse of war powers by using all the tools it has, especially its power to cut funding. It has been encouraging to see Democrats continuing to oppose any supplemental budget request by the administration for the war. It is an area where Democrats have gotten tripped up in the past when they’ve been afraid of accusations that they don’t “support the troops” if they oppose funding for foolish, counterproductive wars. With Democrats having held firm against any additional funding for the war, those days appear to be gone. That is good.

But Democrats need to go further. They should be prepared to oppose all funding for the military, including blocking votes on the National Defense Authorization Act, the annual bill setting out the broad scope and budget for the Defense Department, in order to put an end to hostilities in Iran. In fact, not only should they be willing to withhold funding from the Pentagon, but they should also be willing to withhold funding for the entire government, and threaten another government shutdown if the bill does not prohibit any funding for Trump’s war. December 11 is the deadline for a continuing resolution to keep the government funded and operating. If ever there was a reason for Democrats to threaten to withhold their votes, stopping a blatantly illegal and globally destructive war that American voters have now resoundingly rebuked is it.

Democrats must also be willing to take a hard look at the continuity between Trump’s use of military violence and past uses of force by administrations of both parties, and the bipartisan support for that violence. The groundwork for the Iran war was laid by the Biden administration’s unstinting support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza (as even some former administration officials have acknowledged), but also by years of U.S. refusal to impose any consequences on the Israeli government despite clear evidence of ongoing violations of human rights and international law. Trump’s strikes on alleged “narcoterrorist” drug boats in the Caribbean represent the logical evolution of long-standing treatment of the United States’ drug problem as a “war,” and of casually applying the label of “terrorist” to justify any and all measures, including execution without due process. Seeking accountability for these abuses will require acknowledging the past complicity of both Republicans and Democrats.

Democrats must also take on corruption, a key node connecting the country’s domestic and foreign policy crises. In doing so, they will be walking through an open door. Polls consistently show that political corruption is high on Americans’ list of concerns. According to a recent Harris poll conducted for The Guardian, “Nearly nine out of 10 Americans said that government corruption, as defined as elected officials putting their own or their donors’ financial interests ahead of the public’s, is a problem.” A mid-October CNBC All-America Economic Survey found that voters are more concerned about government corruption than any other issue, including high grocery and gas prices. In September, Gallup reported that “Americans’ perceptions of government corruption in the U.S. are at their highest level in 20 years, with 89% of U.S. adults saying it is widespread.”

To say that the Trump administration provides a target-rich environment for a strong anticorruption push is to commit felony understatement. Exposing foreign gifts to Trump and conflicts of interest by family members, contracts awarded to Trump’s oligarch donors and new tech buddies, and the selling of pardons, as well as restoring enforcement of the Corporate Transparency Act, the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and related task forces, should all be part of the plan. Democrats should drill down into Trump’s wildly corrupt “Board of Peace” for Gaza, which U.S. Representative Jamie Raskin, the Maryland Democrat set to chair the House Judiciary Committee, rightly referred to as a “global slush fund.” The obvious conflicts of interests of Trump’s diplomatic envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner also demand investigation.

The good news is that effective anticorruption does not necessarily require new legislation; it merely requires that existing legislation be enforced. An August 2025 essay in Foreign Affairs, co-authored with my colleagues Casey Michel and Trevor Sutton, laid out a more expansive case for Democrats putting anticorruption at the center of their foreign policy platform. (A recent essay by Casey Michel lays out a more detailed agenda for the new Congress.)

Ultimately, the most important step toward tackling corruption will be reforming the campaign finance system. The United States is an outlier among developed democracies in that its system of campaign finance allows for what is essentially legalized bribery. Legislators speak openly about campaign contributors expecting “returns on investment” for their political donations. This is an outrage. In recent years, foreign actors have increasingly begun bankrolling American legislators, taking advantage of massive loopholes in campaign finance laws and the Federal Election Commission’s lack of enforcement.

Confronting this will be no small task. At a minimum, Congress must move to legislate a response to the Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United decision, which effectively greenlighted bottomless campaign funding from American corporations. It must also reform the Federal Election Commission, providing the body with much-needed resources to investigate campaign finance crimes and restoring the practice of allowing congressional appointments to the commission, which has become little more than an appendage of the executive branch.

All of the above steps must be connected to the top concern among American voters at this moment—the high cost of living. Democrats have disagreements in several policy areas, particularly in foreign policy. Their coalition is diverse. But there is consensus around addressing Americans’ material needs urgently and aggressively. Such an approach would confront Trump’s reckless use of tariffs (while recognizing that the neoliberal taboo on tariffs is a thing of the past), rising gas prices because of the Iran war, the need to restore the global minimum tax, the threat of job losses to AI, and the increased power of tech oligarchs over Americans’ economic and political lives, including on foreign policy, as Elon Musk’s restriction of Ukraine’s Starlink connection demonstrated. The approach should involve a mix of tactics, including hearings, oversight investigations, and legislative proposals.

Many of these efforts may not produce new laws in the next two years. But they could become the backbone of a winning agenda for Congress and for a Democratic administration in 2029. Most important, they would represent a step toward the forging of a new American political consensus on which a new and durable foreign policy can be built.

How Far Will He Go to Make Peace—and War?

#5946. Lame-Duck Trump Heads to Asia

Analysis: Lame-Duck Trump Heads to Asia
